title: Effect of Temperature and Speed on the Formation of Strain-Induced Martensite in AISI 304L and 316L Stainless Steels Subjected to Standardized Tensile Tests
abstract: Abstract With the intention of evaluating the differences in results due to variations in test parameters within ranges standardized by ASTM and ISO, the effect of test speed and temperature were studied for two metastable austenitic stainless steels (grades AISI 304L and AISI 316L). Tensile tests were conducted between 10 °C and 35 °C, strain rates between 2.5 × 10 −4  and 3 × 10 −4  s −1 , and post-yield strain rates between 8.3 × 10 −4  and 7.5 × 10 −3  s −1 . The tendency for the generation of martensitic phase due to plastic deformation within these ranges was measured, as well as the  α ′-martensite content as a function of distance from the fracture zone, modeled as a potential function with a negative exponent. Within the narrow standard parameter ranges tested, a significant trend toward martensitic transformation was found in the AISI 304L alloy, with variations in strength of over 200 MPa (approximately 30 pct between limit parameters), while the AISI 316L alloy showed strength differences of up to 70 MPa (more than 10 pct).

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Austenitic stainless steels are extensively utilized across various industries, ranging from chemical processing to aerospace engineering, and remain a focal point of materials science research due to their exceptional combination of properties, including remarkable corrosion resistance, high strength, and excellent formability. A particular area of research in these materials is devoted to analyzing the deformation-induced martensitic transformation and its corresponding effect on mechanical properties. [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]  In that sense, the study of stress-strain behavior by means of experimental and numerical methods have been used as an approach to understand the formation of strain-induced martensite. The application of mechanical strain ( e.g.,  stainless steel subjected to tensile stress) and corresponding plastic deformation effects favors the formation of martensite nucleation sites, particularly in stainless steels with low stacking fault energy (SFE) values. [ 6 ]  In addition, dislocation pileups at defects (grain boundaries, shear bands, among others) promotes a local concentration of stresses, producing conditions equivalent to those needed for the stress-induced martensitic transformation. [ 7 , 8 ]  Both mechanisms result in the transformation of the austenite (face centered cubic phase) into martensite (body-centered tetragonal or body-centered cubic phase).

Modern metastable systems, such as advanced high strength steels (AHSS), high entropy alloys (HEAs), medium-manganese steels, and certain  β -Titanium alloys face metallurgical challenges similar to those observed in austenitic stainless steels. Strength and ductility balance rely on phase transformation (TRIP), twinning (TWIP), and general austenite to martensite transformation mechanisms. [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]  Recent studies in TRIP-assisted and metastable ferrous alloys have reported similar dependencies of martensitic transformation on strain rate and temperature. [ 12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]  Research on these contemporary materials, especially under dynamic and extreme conditions, highlights the need for a precise characterization of transformation kinetics. Therefore, stress and strain-assisted phase transformation studies in materials such as austenitic stainless steels are relevant for the understanding of transformation mechanisms in these advanced metastable structural materials.
The transformation kinetics also depends on the Stacking Fault Energy (SFE) and the orientation of the parent phase relative to the applied stress. [ 21 ]

Diverse studies in stainless steels have demonstrated that kinetics transformation and deformation-induced martensite content is highly influenced by steel chemical composition, initial grain size, test temperature, strain rate, and stress and strain state. [ 17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ]  Lecroisey and Pineau [ 5 ]  studied the influence of temperature (from − 196 °C to 250 °C) on mechanical behavior in Fe-Ni-Cr steels by conducting tensile tests with a deformation rate of 10 −3  s −1 . They found that mechanical properties are very sensitive to chemical composition and temperature. Furthermore, Martín  et al. [ 22 ]  investigated the deformation-induced microstructures formed in an austenitic stainless steel as a function of temperature (from − 60 °C to 200 °C) at a very low strain rate (0.0004 s −1 ). They concluded that at low temperatures the formation of martensite occurs due to the direct austenite to martensite transformation (fcc to bcc), while at room temperature there is a transformation sequence involving an intermediate martensitic phase (fcc-hcp-bcc) that nucleates at deformation bands. Talonen  et al. [ 23 ]  studied the effect of strain rate (from 3 × 10 −4  to 200 s −1 ) on martensite formation and mechanical properties in AISI 301LN and AISI 304 stainless steels. They found that the strain rate promotes adiabatic heating which in turn suppresses the strain-induced austenite to martensite transformation. In addition, Lichtenfeld  et al. [ 24 ]  studied the relationship between martensitic transformation and strain rate at test speeds as high as 400 s −1 . Particularly, they analyzed the influence of strain rate on test sample heating and corresponding effect on martensite content and tensile strength. They also studied the relationship between stacking fault energy (SFE) and test temperature. Okayasu  et al. [ 25 ]  investigated the strain-induced martensitic transformation in a SUS304 stainless steel by conducting tensile tests with different load levels at room temperature. By analyzing the evolution of the sample microstructure from the fracture surface they found that even in the low plastic strain regime strain-induced martensitic transformation occurs; with the martensite content increasing dramatically after the ultimate strength point. In addition, Behera  et al. [ 26 ]  studied the nucleation mechanism of strain-induced martensite in 304LN stainless steels at room temperature by means of tensile tests at different strain rates. They found that the martensite content decreases as the strain rate increases due to sample heating. Comparable strain-rate–driven suppression of martensite formation has also been reported in metastable steels subjected to controlled deformation conditions. [ 27 ]  As proposed by Olson and Cohen, [ 21 ]  an increase in sample temperature will reduce the tendency for martensite formation, as it reduces the density of slip faults, which act as nucleation sites.

Different methods can be used to measure martensite content in a stainless steel. Particularly, Talonen  et al. [ 28 ]  conducted a study comparing ferritoscope measurements with those obtained with five other techniques for quantifying strain-induced martensite contents in AISI 301LN and AISI 304L steels. They found that X-ray diffraction exhibits a strong correlation with ferritoscope measurements. However, the X-ray analysis is restricted to a thin surface layer and can be challenging to use in sheet materials subjected to plastic deformation or when the martensite phase is not uniformly distributed, as in the case of specimens subjected to tensile test. The Satmagan technique provides good measurement correlations, but it also requires a uniform martensite distribution in the sample. Magnetic balance technique and density measurements techniques were also used in the comparison; the former is very sensitive to specimen thickness and it is strongly affected by surface roughness and curvature, while the latter lacks satisfactory reproducibility. Optical microscopy proved to be an applicable technique for detecting martensite. However, the investigation demonstrated that martensite contents could be overestimated. They concluded that ferritometric method, with an appropriate correction factor, is a reliable tool to determine strain-induced martensite contents, up to 90 pct. In addition, the ferritometric method allows to take measurement at different sample locations, which is particularly useful in specimens with variable martensite distribution. This method has also been verified by other researchers. [ 29 ]

The strain-induced martensite content and corresponding mechanical behavior of AISI 304L and AISI316L samples subjected to tensile tests have been evaluated in this investigation. In particular, the tests have been conducted within a narrow range of standardized parameters established by ASTM and ISO. [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ]  In that sense, this investigation covers a set of parameters that have not been previously analyzed or reported, demonstrating that mechanical properties could be significantly modified by slight variations in test parameters, which in turn might strongly affect the results of quality requirements evaluation in a typical engineering project. Therefore, this investigation contributes to the research subject by generating data for the case of austenitic stainless steels with a low carbon content.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Two grades of commercial austenitic stainless steel were used for the investigation: AISI 304L and AISI 316L. Chemical composition was experimentally determined using a Bruker Magellan Q8 optical emission spectrometer. Both steels were supplied as 3 mm thick cold-rolled sheets in the fully annealed, pickled, and skin passed condition. The Ms temperature, which denotes the starting of the direct austenite to martensite transformation, was estimated using the Eichelman and Hull formula. [ 17 ]  In addition, the Md 30  temperature, which corresponds to the temperature at which 50 pct of martensite is formed at a tensile strain of 0.3, was estimated using the formula provided by Nohara  et al. [ 20 ]  The microstructure was evaluated preparing samples for both steels according to ASTM E3. [ 33 ]  An electroetching process using 10 pct oxalic acid for 20 seconds at 3 V was performed to reveal the phases. Grain size was evaluated using the comparative method outlined in ASTM E112. [ 34 ]

sections.heading: Tensile Testing
paragraphs: Tensile tests were conducted using a Z250 Zwick Roell electromechanical testing machine, with a 250 kN capacity. The testing standards selected for this study included ASTM E8/E8M-22, [ 30 ]  ASTM A370-21, [ 30 ]  and ISO 6892-1:2009. [ 32 ]  The test conditions were adjusted to the intersection of the ranges specified by these standards, ensuring consistency and comparability of the results. Three temperature values (10 °C, 23 °C, and 35 °C) were selected, which corresponded to the common overlap of the normalized ambient temperature ranges defined in the three specifications. Normalized room temperature was maintained throughout the test by using a forced air chamber where the tests were conducted. The temperature control system operated within a margin of ± 1 °C from the set temperature. The specimen geometry corresponds to the standard size according to ASTM. [ 30 , 31 ]  Testing started once the specimen reached thermal equilibrium. Localized temperature measurements were attempted by mounting K-type thermocouples on the sample surface at the mid-length of the reduced section. However, fracture occurred at a random position in the gauge length and it did not necessarily coincide with the thermocouple position. Since it was not possible to consistently record the temperature peak associated with necking and fracture, the analysis was conducted considering the normalized room temperature registered in the testing chamber. The engineering strain was calculated from the change in distance between reference marks placed along the reduced section of the specimen (initial length: 50 mm). This method is depicted in the corresponding standards and is consistent with testing and certification practices.

Strain rate (per mm of reduced section), expressed as test speed, was determined in accordance with the aforementioned standards. The applied strain-rate ranges, which simultaneously comply with ISO and ASTM specifications, are summarized in Table  I . Three values were selected and arbitrarily designated as low, medium, and high speeds. It should be noted that minor variations in the strain rate for yield-strength determination were intentionally introduced to maintain full compliance with ASTM and ISO requirements. Three specimens were tested for each temperature–strain-rate condition.
 Table I Strain Rate (mm/mm/min) Strain Rate Up to Yield Point Strain Rate After Yield Point Low Speed Med Speed High Speed Low Speed Med Speed High Speed 0.015 min −1  (2.5 × 10 −4  S −1 ) 0.0165 min −1  (2.75 × 10 −4  S −1 ) 0.018 min −1  (3 × 10 −4  S −1 ) 0.05 min −1  (8.3 × 10 −4  S −1 ) 0.265 min −1  (4.42 × 10 −3  S −1 ) 0.45 min −1  (7.5 × 10 −3  S −1 ) Strain rates are expressed in min −1  to reflect the requirements of ASTM E8/E8M-22 and ASTM A370-21 standards; equivalent values in s −1  are provided to facilitate comparison with the scientific literature.

Data acquisition and processing were performed using the Zwick Roell testXpert II software and results were statistically analyzed. The influence of temperature and strain rate on the mechanical properties ( σ 0.2 , UTS, and total elongation) was assessed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with replication. Temperature and strain rate were treated as independent variables, while the mechanical properties were considered as dependent variables. Statistical significance was determined at a 95 pct confidence level ( p  < 0.05) employing three replicates for each testing condition.

sections.heading: Martensite Content Measurement
paragraphs: Ferritometric measurements were performed on the as-tested surface condition, without any previous mechanical o chemical treatment, in order to avoid the generation of surface irregularities and inconsistency.

In addition, martensite content was evaluated by X-ray diffraction method. XRD analysis was performed using a BRUKER D8 DISCOVER instrument with Cu K α  radiation, a 1 second dwell time, and a 0.02° step size. The 316L material samples were examined before and after a pickling process performed to assess the preexistence of martensite in the microstructure, due to a cold working process. Pickling was performed using a 1:1:1 mixture of HCl, HNO 3 , and distilled H 2 O at 20 °C, resulting in a pickling-induced thickness reduction of 0.460 mm. The samples were immersed in the acidic solution for 35 minutes to remove any surface layer that might contain martensite resulting from sheet forming. This deep cleaning process guaranteed the removal of residual martensite and surface residues and was considered appropriate for XRD analysis.

sections.heading: Tensile Test
paragraphs: Figure  2  shows representative tensile stress-strain curves obtained for the analyzed steels, at a different temperature and at the same strain rate (medium speed, 4.42 × 10 −3  s −1 ). The effect of test temperature in strength is remarkable; maximum tensile strength decreases as temperature increases. A reduction of approximately 110 and 70 MPa was registered by varying the test temperature from 10 °C to 35 °C, for the AISI304L and 316L stainless, correspondingly. The variations in slope reflect changes in the kinetics of martensitic transformation under the different testing conditions. The hardening rate is more pronounced at low temperatures and low strain rates, which is attributed to an increased formation of  α ′-martensite, a characteristic mechanism of the Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect. [ 36 ]  This behavior is consistent with previous findings in metastable austenitic steels. Furthermore, the stress–strain curves exhibit continuous yielding behavior without a distinct yield point, indicating that plastic deformation proceeds smoothly from the onset of loading. This observation suggests that martensitic transformation initiates progressively during plastic flow rather than being triggered at a distinct stress level. [ 24 ] Fig. 2 Stress strain curves for 304L (left group) and 316L (right group) specimens at medium speed

Figure  3  presents yield and tensile strength, as well as percentage of elongation, as a function of strain rate and temperature for the whole set of samples. The error bars representing ± 1 standard deviation ( n  = 3). Fig. 3 Influence of strain rate for 304L (left column) and 316L (right column) specimens

For the AISI 304L steel, a noticeable increase in tensile strength with decreasing strain rate and temperature is observed. The maximum value of tensile strength (815 MPa) corresponds to a strain rate of 8.3 × 10 −4  s −1  and a temperature of 10 °C. Furthermore, the lowest value (613 MPa) corresponds to a strain rate of 7.5 × 10 −3  s −1  and a temperature of 35 °C. For all testing speeds the yield strength remains constant for the temperatures of 35 °C and 23 °C. A slight increase with strain rate is observed when comparing the value for a temperature of 10 °C to those obtained for the same temperature and higher strain rate values. For all test speeds, the maximum value of elongation is observed for the temperature of 35 °C. The difference in elongation values for the rest of the conditions falls within error margin. Therefore, no particular correlation between test speed, temperature, and percentage of elongation was found for these samples. For the AISI 316L, the trend of increasing tensile strength with decreasing test temperature and strain rate is maintained. However, the difference between maximum and minimum values is not as high as in the case of the AISI304L steel (75 MPa compared to 202 MPa for the AISI 304L). For a given test temperature, the values of yield strength remain constant. However, there is a clear difference between the values obtained for 10 °C compared to those for 23 °C and 35 °C (approximately 50 MPa). In contrast to the AISI304L, the maximum values of elongation are obtained for a temperature of 10 °C, and for a strain rate of 8.3 × 10 −4  s −1 .

sections.heading: Martensite Content
paragraphs: Figure  5  shows the relationship between  α ′-martensite content and the mechanical properties for the AISI 304L stainless steel. The presented values of martensite correspond to those obtained at a distance of 3 mm from the fracture surface. As expected, a direct correlation is observed between the final α′-martensite content and the Ultimate Tensile Strength ( σ UTS ), since the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect enhances the load-bearing capacity up to failure. In contrast, the Yield Strength ( σ 0.2 ) remains nearly constant and shows no correlation with the final martensite content. This behavior is consistent, as most of the  α ′-martensite forms after yielding through a predominantly strain-induced mechanism. If the transformation were stress-assisted, a stronger correlation with  σ 0.2  would be expected. The lack of such dependence within the present testing range therefore validates the deformation-controlled nature of the transformation. Fig. 5 Mechanical properties  vs  amount of  α ′-martensite (pct vol) at 3 mm from surface fracture for 304L stainless steel

The elongation percentage increases slightly with the martensite content up to 50–60 pct content and then decreases. Figure  6  presents the effect of temperature on martensite formation, considering the registered value at a position of 3 mm from the fracture surface. Overall, for a given velocity, as the temperature decreases the content of martensite increases. Fig. 6 Variation of  α ′-martensite (pct mass) with test temperature for 304L stainless steel

Figure  7  presents the martensite content as a function of the distance ( d ) from the fracture surface for the AISI 316L steel. As in the case of the AISI 304L steel, the maximum content of martensite is evidenced near the fracture surface; as the distance from that area increases the martensite percentage decreases. In particular, a content of approximately 35 pct is attained for a strain rate and temperature of 8.3 × 10 −4  s −1  and 10 °C, respectively. For any given speed, the samples tested at 10 °C always exhibit the biggest amount for martensite. The  α ′-martensite content also follows a potential curve as defined by Eq. [ 2 ], but with a steeper negative exponent compared to that for the AISI 304L steel. Since the value of the exponent is larger, the  α ′-martensite content decreases more rapidly with the distance from the fracture surface. Fig. 7 Amount of  α ′-martensite (pct mass)  vs  distance (d) from fracture surface for 316L stainless steel

As seen in Figure  8 , XRD measurements confirm that the phase detected by the ferritoscope is indeed alpha martensite, with characteristics peaks at (110), (200), and (211), particularly in 316L steel since the detected martensite contents were lower compared to 304L steel. Fig. 8 XRD pattern confirming the presence of  α ′-martensite with characteristic peaks at (110), (200), and (211) for 316L stainless steel

Figure  9  shows the relation between martensite content (measured at 3 mm from the fracture surface) and tensile and yield strength, as well as percentage of elongation. Although there is a monotonic increase in tensile strength with martensite content, the magnitude of that increment is considerably lower compared to that observed for the AISI 304L stainless steel. This is consistent with the smaller amount of martensite formed. The percentage of elongation exhibits a very well-defined increase with martensite content. Yield strength does not exhibit a particular trend, due to the same reason as that for the AISI 304L. Finally, Figure  10  presents the effect of temperature on martensite formation (value measured at 3 mm from the fracture surface). Consistently, the lower the test temperature and speed, the higher the value of martensite content. Fig. 9 Mechanical properties  vs  Amount of  α ′-martensite (pct mass) for 316L stainless steel Fig. 10 Variation of  α ′-martensite (pct mass) with test temperature for 316L stainless steel

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The results show that small variations in tensile test parameters within standardized ambient ranges can produce significant changes in the metallurgical and mechanical behavior of metastable austenitic stainless steels. In AISI 304L, reducing the test temperature from 35 °C to 10 °C and the strain rate from 7.5 × 10 −3  s −1  to 8.3 × 10 −4  s −1  led to differences of about 200 MPa in tensile strength and roughly 50 pct in  α ′-martensite content. In AISI 316L, the same variations produced smaller changes, consistent with its higher austenite stability.

The  α ′-martensite content decreases with distance from the fracture zone, following a power law with a negative exponent, confirming that transformation is most intense in the necking region where local strain is maximum. The decay exponent ( n ) in Eq. [ 4 ] represents the sensitivity of the deformation-induced martensitic transformation ( α ′) to the non-uniform plastic strain distribution along the specimen gauge length. The difference in n between AISI 304L and 316L is associated with their intrinsic austenite stability. The 316L steel exhibits a lower Md 30  temperature and therefore higher stability, requiring a greater plastic strain energy for  α ′ nucleation. This results in a less pronounced spatial gradient of  α ′, with martensite concentrated near the region of maximum deformation (close to the fracture). Conversely, the less stable 304L forms  α ′ over a broader deformation zone, producing a steeper decay of  α ′ along the reduced section.

The temperature effect aligns with the proximity of the Md 30  temperature for 304L (~39 °C) to the test range. Lower temperatures enhance the driving force for transformation, whereas higher temperatures inhibit it due to lower slip-fault density and greater austenite stability.

Although direct in situ temperature measurements could not be quantified due to random fracture locations within the reduced section, exploratory monitoring confirmed local heating during plastic deformation. This heating arises from both plastic work and the exothermic nature of the martensitic transformation. As reported by Lichtenfeld  et al. [ 24 ]  and Vázquez-Fernández  et al. [ 38 ]  such effects occur even under quasi-isothermal conditions at low strain rates (8.3 × 10 −4 –7.5 × 10 −3  s −1 ). However, since these rates are below the adiabatic regime (≥ 0.1 s −1 ), the generated heat is partially dissipated, contributing locally to austenite stabilization without producing a fully adiabatic condition.

The absence of a distinct yield point in the stress–strain curves further supports the progressive nature of the transformation under the current conditions. Smooth yielding behavior is characteristic of strain-induced martensitic transformation, [ 13 , 15 , 16 , 30 ]  where nucleation occurs gradually during plastic flow through the accumulation of stacking faults and shear bands. Conversely, stress-assisted transformation typically produces discrete yield points near the Ms temperature, where the chemical driving force is sufficiently high. Under the low strain rates (≈2.5–3.0 × 10 −4  s −1 ) and narrow temperature range (10–35 °C) employed in this study, martensite forms progressively, which is consistent with the observed continuous work-hardening behavior.

The distinctive strain-hardening response observed in Figure  2  provides indirect yet compelling evidence of the influence of deformation-induced martensitic transformation on plastic flow. As described by Olson and Cohen [ 21 ]  and Lichtenfeld  et al. [ 24 ]  the progressive formation of  α ′-martensite during plastic deformation contributes to sustained work hardening and delays the onset of necking. The behavior observed in AISI 304L therefore reflects the interaction between austenite stability and transformation kinetics within the investigated temperature and strain-rate ranges.

The effect of strain rate on deformation-induced martensitic transformation (DIMT) stems from a combination of both thermal and kinetic mechanisms that occur even under near-isothermal conditions. [ 12 , 14 ]  Both plastic deformation and martensitic transformation generate heat, which locally raises the temperature and stabilizes the austenite, thereby reducing the driving force for the transformation. Although the strain rates used are below the adiabatic regime, measurable temperature increases can still occur, which partially suppresses martensite nucleation. [ 38 ]  Kinetically, low strain rates allow for the rearrangement and interaction of dislocations, stacking faults, and shear bands, thus enhancing the nucleation of  α ′-martensite. [ 3 , 21 , 37 ]  Conversely, higher strain rates limit the evolution of defects and increase localized heating, restricting the transformation. Therefore, the strain rate dependence of DIMT in metastable steels results from the interaction of thermal and kinetic factors that modulate both the driving force and the nucleation density.

It is important to emphasize that the applied strain rates are significantly below the threshold (∼0.1 s −1 ) at which adiabatic conditions have been reported in austenitic stainless steels. [ 24 , 38 ]  Within the non-adiabatic regime under which this study was conducted, the temperature rise is primarily attributed to plastic work and the exothermic nature of the martensitic transformation. [ 39 ]

These results demonstrate that, even within the narrow “ambient” ranges defined by ASTM and ISO standards, [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ]  variations in temperature and strain rate can significantly alter the tensile properties. These standards, which are adequate for conventional materials where strengthening is dislocation-driven, are less reliable for materials whose constitutive behavior is coupled with deformation-induced transformation (TRIP/DIMT). In such cases, minor changes in temperature or strain rate can strongly affect the formation of  α ′-martensite and, consequently, the resulting mechanical properties. For these materials, material test reports (MTRs) should explicitly indicate the exact testing temperature (T) and the strain rate (ϵ˙) to ensure quality consistency, interlaboratory reproducibility, and the optimization of forming processes sensitive to ambient conditions.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Small variations in temperature and strain rate, even within the narrow standard ranges defined by ASTM and ISO specifications, produce significant changes in the mechanical response and the kinetics of deformation-induced martensitic transformation in metastable austenitic stainless steels. AISI 304L exhibited the highest sensitivity; depending on testing conditions a difference of about 200 MPa in tensile strength and martensite content can be obtained. In contrast, AISI 316L showed smaller variations (up to 70 MPa), consistent with its greater austenite stability. The distribution of  α ′-martensite from fracture end in samples follows a decreasing potential function curve, confirming that the necking region experiences the highest level of transformation. The exponential decay was steeper in 316L, reflecting its lower transformation tendency. These findings challenge the implicit expectation in standardized testing protocols that mechanical property variations should remain small within the “ambient” range. While current ASTM and ISO standards acknowledge that parameters such as temperature and strain rate may have an effect, they do not explore or explicitly warn about the magnitude of this influence in metastable austenitic steels near their Md 30  temperature. These results highlight the need to refine testing standards and reporting practices to reduce scatter and to improve the correlation between measured properties and in-service performance.
